latin.499: §. IV. Ita habet Commentarius verborum Institutionis S. Cœnæ Antecedaneus, Sententiæ de ea veræ tam originem dans, quàm fundamentum struens, ab ipso Christo confectus, quem excipit Succedaneus Apostolicus, speciatim Paulinus 1. Cor. 10. & 11. capp. Horum Capitum prius quàm plurima pro spirituali corporis & sanguinis Christi præsentia & participatione, nullum verò pro corporali suppeditat argumentum.
latin.500: Primum desumtum à Communione & participatione Christi, eòque corporis & sanguinis Christi (quibus sine Christus ne Christus quidem est) Veteris Testamenti Christianis impertita, de quibus Apostolus versu 1. Non vult nos ignorare, omnes eandem escam spiritualem edisse, omnes item eundem potum spiritualem bibisse, puta non inter se tantum omnes, sed & nobiscum; Nam immediatè sequitur: Bibebant enim ex sequenti spirituali Petra; Petra verò erat Christus; Sed de hoc solo & nosmet Christiani N. T., sanguinem ejus spiritualiter bibimus, sicuti & escam spiritualem, Mannam de cœlo descendentem, i. e. Christum ejusque corpus, nec quicquam aliud, itidem cum Patribus V. Test. participamus, Sacramentis Veterum, quoad Signa quidem, à nostris, diversis, quoad Significata verò iisdem existentibus, dicente Augustino Tract. 26. super Johannem, juxta istud Petrinum: Quin verò, per Gratiam Domini nostri Jesu Christi, credimus nos Salvatum iri, kath' hon tropon kakeinoi. Act. 15, 11.
latin.501: Exceptioni seu Dubio: Quâ ratione Veteres Christum eô, quô nos, in sacramentis modô, perceperint, cum Filius Dei eô tempore nondum carnem assumsisset, neque sanguis ab eo effusus exstaret, egregiè occurrit Petrus Martyr, Comment. in hunc locum: Quoad DEUM, inquit, (addo etiam quoad homines fideles & spiritualem eorum manducationem) Mors Christi & Sanguinis ejus effusio & carnis assumtio, semper fuerunt præsentia, rata, placita & accepta. Quare in Apocalypsi dicitur Agnus ab origine mundi occisus: nec non ad Hebræos, Christus heri ac hodiè ac in æternum. Et de Abrahamo pronunciatur in Evangelio, quod Christi diem viderit & lætatus sit. Unde non est firma ea connexio, caro & sanguis Christi nondum per Œconomiam seu dispensationem temporis fuerant assumta, non potuerunt ergo esse Veteribus spiritualis cibus & potus. Nam cùm salus Patrum, quemadmodum nostra, penderet à morte & sanguine Christi, oporteat eos, ut nos, ista fide complecti, alioquin salutem non habuissent. Mors, caro, & sanguis Christi, tametsi non adhuc exstabant in natura, (addo, naturaliter scilicet ac corporaliter, spiritualiter tamen & supernaturaliter non minùs atque nunc, postquam naturaliter localiterque cælum occupat, nec per descensum naturalem Cœnis nostris sacris sese immiscet) attamen ad servandos Patres vim ac efficaciam habere potuerunt. Unde pro ratione sui temporis in suis Sacramentis illa eadem quæ nos consequebantur. Divinam personam, id est, filium Dei præsentem habebant, quem fide complectebantur, & quidem cum hac promissione, vel, ut ita dicam, cum hoc respectu ad humanam naturam, quod eam esset assumturus: Atque hoc discrimen est inter Christum, quòd ipsi accipiebant & quòd modò nos sumimus: Nam quod illi per fidem faciendum præsentiebant, nos jam factum confitemur. Hic idem Martyr duabus præterea speciosis admodum Objectionibus … planissimè & solidissimè satisfacit.
latin.502: Alterum Argumentum ex decimo Capite prioris Epistolæ ad Corinthios, desumtum, ab ea Communione poculi benedictionis cum sanguine Christi, & ea communione panis fracti cum corpore Christi petitum est, quæ similis existit communioni & in unum corpus coalitiioni eorum, qui ejusdem panis Dominici, vel etiam tou henos artou cum articulo, i. e. ejusdem panis spiritualis, seu Christi Domini ipsius participes fiunt? Ita enim Christus vers. 16. & 17. Poculum benedictionis, cui benedicimus, nonne communicatio sanguinis Christi est? panis quem frangimus, nonne communicatio corporis Christi est? Nam unus est panis, unum corpus multi sumus: nam omnes ex eodem pane participamus. At horum Unio in idem corpus communioque, non est corporalis, sed Spiritualis.
latin.503: Subjicitur Tertium Argumentum versu proximo 18. à Communione Israëlitarum sacrificantium & ex sacrificiis pacificis comedentium, cum ipso Deo ejusque Altari; Itemque Quartum vers. 20. & 21. à Communione Gentium, Dæmoniis immolantium & horum mensæ participantium, cum ipsis Dæmoniis, haustum, his Apostoli verbis: Cernite Israelem qui est secundum carnem: Nonne qui edunt victimas, consortes fiunt altaris? Imò verò dico, quæ immolant Gentes Dæmoniis immolant: Nolim autem vos consortes Dæmoniorum esse. Utraque verò Communio, tum Israëlitarum Deo sacrificantium cum Deo ejusque altari, tùm gentium Dæmoniis immolantium mensæque horum communicantium, cum Diabolo & hujus Mensa, non Corporalis exinde, sed Spiritualis, maximè interim realis erat & substantialis.
latin.504: Posterius seu Undecimum ad Corinthios caput Pauli, eatenus potissimum veræ Sententiæ de S. Cœna fundandæ inservit, quòd Paulus in eo, ex ore Christi, Institutionis verba, idque cum emphatica quâdam interpretatione repetit, quâ & panem non simpliciter Corpus Christi, sed corpus pro nobis fractum vers. 24.; Poculum verò, seu vinum in poculo, non simpliciter sanguinem Christi, sed Novum illud pactum per sanguinem suum vers. 25. salutat (hôc pacto Propositiones Sacramentales improprias seu tropicas luculentissimo modo declarans, præsentiam interim ac participationem, tam corporis, quàm carnis Christi spiritualem, neutiquam inficiatus) in sequentibus immediatè versiculis tribus 26. 27. & 28., Sacramentum S. Cœnæ ex duabus rebus, cœlesti & terrestri, non minus, post, quàm ante consecrationis dicta vulgò verba, constare, nec harum alteram in alterius substantiam i. e. panem & vinum in corpus & sanguinem Christi, converti aut transmutari edocturus, panem crebriùs & poculum ingeminat, dicens: Quotiescunque ederitis panem hunc & poculum hoc biberitis &c. Itaque quisquis ederit panem hunc indignè &c. Exploret autem quisque seipsum & edat de pane hoc. &c.

pass_a.499: §. IV. So stands the Antecedent Commentary on the Institution words of the Sacred Supper, giving both origin and foundation to the true sentence concerning it, composed by Christ Himself, which the Apostolic Successor receives — specially the Pauline chapters 1 Cor. 10 and 11. The former of these chapters supplies as many arguments as you please for the spiritual presence and participation of Christ’s body and blood, but none for the corporal.
pass_a.500: The first is taken from the Communion and participation of Christ — and so of Christ’s body and blood (without which Christ is not even Christ) — imparted to Old Testament Christians, of whom the Apostle at v. 1 does not want us ignorant that all ate the same spiritual food and drank the same spiritual drink, not only among themselves but with us; For it immediately follows: For they drank of the spiritual Rock that followed; and the Rock was Christ; But of this alone we New Testament Christians also drink His blood spiritually, as also the spiritual food, the Manna descending from heaven, i.e. Christ and His body, and nothing else, participating likewise with the Fathers of the Old Testament, the sacraments of the ancients differing from ours as to Signs, but the same as to Signifieds — Augustine Tract. 26 on John, following Peter: But we believe that through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ we shall be saved, even as they. (Acts 15:11).
pass_a.501: To the exception or doubt — how the ancients perceived Christ in the sacraments in the same mode as we, when the Son of God had not yet assumed flesh nor had blood been poured out — Petrus Martyr answers excellently: As to GOD (I add also as to faithful men and their spiritual eating) Christ’s death and the pouring of His blood and assumption of flesh were always present, ratified, pleasing and accepted. Hence in the Apocalypse the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world; and to the Hebrews, Christ yesterday and today and forever; and of Abraham in the Gospel, that he saw Christ’s day and rejoiced. So the inference that flesh and blood not yet assumed by the economy of time could not be spiritual food and drink for the ancients is not firm … The Fathers had the divine Person present by faith with promise of the nature to be assumed; the difference is that they foresaw by faith what was to be done, we confess it already done. The same Martyr also most plainly and solidly satisfies two further specious objections.
pass_a.502: The Second Argument from the tenth chapter of the former Epistle to the Corinthians is taken from that Communion of the cup of blessing with Christ’s blood, and that communion of the broken bread with Christ’s body, which is like the communion and coalescence into one body of those who become partakers of the same Lord’s bread — or even of the one bread with the article, i.e. of the same spiritual bread, or of Christ the Lord Himself? So Christ at vv. 16–17: The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ? the bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ? For we being many are one bread, one body: for we all partake of that one bread. But their Union into the same body and communion is not corporal, but Spiritual.
pass_a.503: There follows a Third Argument at the next verse 18 from the Communion of sacrificing Israelites eating of peace-offerings with God Himself and His Altar; and likewise a Fourth at vv. 20–21 from the Communion of the Gentiles sacrificing to demons and partaking of their table with the demons themselves … But both Communions — of Israelites sacrificing to God with God and His altar, and of Gentiles sacrificing to demons and communicating at their table with the Devil and his Table — were thence not Corporal but Spiritual, yet meantime most real and substantial.
pass_a.504: The latter or Eleventh chapter to the Corinthians serves chiefly to found the true Sentence concerning the Sacred Supper in that Paul there repeats from Christ’s mouth the Institution words with a certain emphatic interpretation, whereby he greets the bread not simply as Christ’s Body but as the body broken for us (v. 24); and the Cup, or wine in the cup, not simply as Christ’s blood but as that New covenant through His blood (v. 25) — thereby declaring most lucidly that the Sacramental Propositions are improper or tropical, meanwhile by no means denying spiritual presence and participation of Christ’s body and flesh — and in the three verses immediately following 26–28, about to teach that the Sacrament of the Sacred Supper consists of two things, celestial and terrestrial, no less after than before the words commonly called consecration, and that neither is converted or transmuted into the other’s substance, i.e. bread and wine into Christ’s body and blood, he more often doubles bread and cup, saying: As often as you eat this bread and drink this cup &c. Therefore whoever shall eat this bread unworthily &c. But let a man examine himself and so eat of this bread. &c.

499: §.IV: Christ’s antecedent Institution commentary (origin and foundation of the true sentence) is succeeded by the Apostolic / Pauline commentary — specially 1 Cor. 10 and 11.
Chapter 10 supplies many arguments for spiritual presence and participation of body and blood — none for the corporal.
500: First argument: OT believers already shared Christ’s communion — the same spiritual food and drink (1 Cor. 10:1–4); the Rock was Christ.
We NT Christians drink His blood spiritually and share the same spiritual food — Christ and His body — with the Fathers; signs differ, significata are the same (Augustine; Acts 15:11).
501: Objection: how could ancients receive Christ sacramentally before flesh assumed and blood shed? Petrus Martyr: before God (and for faithful spiritual eating) death, blood-shedding, and flesh-assumption were always present and accepted — Lamb slain from the world’s foundation; Christ yesterday and forever; Abraham saw His day.

Flesh not yet in nature corporally could still save the Fathers spiritually; they held the Son by faith under promise of the nature to be assumed — we confess what they foresaw as already done. Martyr also answers two further specious objections solidly.
502: Second argument (1 Cor. 10:16–17): communion of the cup of blessing with Christ’s blood and of the broken bread with His body is like coalescing into one body as partakers of the one spiritual bread — Christ Himself.
That union into one body is not corporal but Spiritual.
503: Third (v. 18): Israel’s sacrificers eating peace-offerings are partners of the altar with God — a spiritual, yet most real and substantial, communion.
Fourth (vv. 20–21): Gentile demon-sacrificers share the demons’ table — likewise spiritual, not corporal, yet real; Paul will not have us partners of demons.
504: 1 Cor. 11 chiefly founds the true Supper sentence: Paul repeats Institution from Christ’s mouth with emphasis — bread as body broken for us (v. 24); cup as the New covenant through His blood (v. 25) — tropical propositions, without denying spiritual presence and participation.
Vv. 26–28: the sacrament is two things, celestial and terrestrial, after consecration as before — bread and wine are not converted into body and blood; he keeps saying this bread / this cup.
Stop before §.V (Pauline true sentence lasting through the Apostolic first age).
